name: Baryta Yellow
lede: Baryta yellow is barium chromate, a dull greenish yellow pigment with a heap of trade names; the swatch in our library is a pale straw that stands for it.

sections.title: One compound, many names
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium says baryta yellow is Heaton's 1928 synonym for barium chromate [1]. The same pigment was sold as barium yellow, lemon yellow, permanent yellow, Steinbuhl yellow, ultramarine yellow and yellow ultramarine [2].

Books disagree over some of those names. Rose (1916) gives Steinbuhl yellow as a synonym for baryta yellow, but Kuhn and Curran add that in Germany the name was also applied to calcium chromate [3]. Jannicke (1893), Linke and Adam (1913) and Rose all say it is wrong to call barium chromate ultramarine yellow [4].

sections.title: Not the baryta white
sections.body: Barium chromate is a different material from baryte, the barium sulfate used as a white filler [5]. In the 1940s the National Lead Company developed a barium potassium chromate for anti-corrosion paint [6].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The library records the color from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, the 1955 ISCC-NBS system and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and its near-twin there is Chartreuse Yellow, about one unit away [7]. The swatch is a pale straw, nearest to [[beige]] among everyday names [7]. A flat swatch cannot show the greenish cast the Colour Index gives the pigment ('dull, greenish yellow'), and the sources give no color values for it [2][7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This pale yellow is common in museum paintings: 665 of 23,781, or 2.8 per cent, hold it over at least five per cent of the canvas [8]. It peaks in the 1840s, in 44 of 699 paintings, and Turner carries it in 4 of 14 [8]. Because it is a pale straw that also describes aged varnish, the match is not evidence of the pigment, and these are photographs, not tests [8].
